issues.legal_issue: A conclusive statutory declaration that a listed religious institution is of a particular faith does not violate constitutional rights where a claimant may still seek adjudication of a claim to the physical property as private property or as property of another institution.
material_facts: A shrine was listed in the statute and declared to be a religious institution of the specified faith.
A claimant alleged that the shrine was instead associated with another religious order and challenged the conclusive effect of the declaration.

The State and the religious management body accepted that claims could be made to the listed property, including the building, as private property or as property of another institution, and that such claims could be adjudicated by the tribunal.
issues.conclusion: The conclusive effect of the declaration did not violate the claimant’s rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and 26 because a claim to the property remained open for adjudication.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(4) of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925, read consistently with the interpretation permitting claims to the physical property, was not unconstitutional under Articles 19(1)(f) and 26. A provision should be construed, where possible, to sustain its constitutionality; the Court also relied on the presumption of constitutionality and the principle of stare decisis for a long-standing construction of a local statute. It referred to the decisions in Mahant Davinder Singh v. Shromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, Raj Narain Pandey v. Sant Prasad Tewari, and Brownsea Haven Properties v. Poole Corporation, and to the earlier tribunal interpretation concerning Gurdwara Rupar.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_religious_pr: A claimant brings a constitutional challenge to a law’s classification of a religious institution.
predicates.institution_listed_and_declared_by_law: The institution is listed under the law and declared to belong to the specified religious category.
predicates.claimant_can_seek_adjudication_of_physic: The claimant is permitted to ask the designated adjudicator to determine whether the physical property belongs privately or to another institution.

issues.definition: When an institution is listed and declared by law, the classification does not unconstitutionally bar a property claim if a claimant may still seek adjudication of that claim.

issues.legal_issue: Publication of a statutory notification can provide sufficient notice for proceedings concerning a religious institution without individual service on every affected person.
material_facts: The appeals concerned properties covered by notifications under Section 7 that were not included in the statute’s First Schedule.
The appellants complained that the notification had merely been published and that individual notice had not been given to them.
The statutory process provided a means for persons claiming rights in the notified property to present their claims.
issues.conclusion: The complaint that publication alone was insufficient notice was rejected, and the statutory procedure was not invalid on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: The maxim audi alteram partem does not require individual service in every statutory proceeding. The Court considered the purpose and procedure of the Act, including its notification and claims process, and relied on the majority decision in Municipal Board, Hapur, in addressing whether publication could constitute adequate notice.

predicates.challenge_to_publicly_notified_religious: A person challenges a statutory proceeding concerning property identified through public notification.
predicates.statute_provides_publication_and_claim_p: The governing procedure calls for publication and provides a process for persons to submit claims concerning the property.
predicates.individual_notice_not_served: The affected person was not separately served with individual notice.

issues.definition: Where a statutory process publicly notifies property and allows claims concerning it, publication can be sufficient even if individual notice was not served.

issues.legal_issue: A person who does not claim ownership of the institution and has not established a sufficient legal interest cannot maintain a constitutional writ challenge to its statutory classification.
material_facts: The claimant alleged that he was associated with a religious order different from the one specified in the declaration and claimed an interest in the property.
The High Court found that he had not claimed ownership of the institution as defined in the statute, and the majority rejected the challenge.
In a separate opinion, Khanna J. considered the claimant’s alleged possession and pending property claim sufficient to bring the writ petition, while agreeing that the appeal should be dismissed.
issues.conclusion: The majority rejected the claimant’s challenge on the basis that he had not established the right or interest required to maintain it; Khanna J. disagreed on standing but agreed with dismissal of the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226, a claimant must establish a legally sufficient interest to maintain a writ petition. The majority accepted the High Court’s finding that the claimant had not claimed ownership of the institution; Khanna J.’s separate opinion considered the alleged possession and pending claim sufficient for standing, leaving the merits of the property claim to the tribunal.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenging_religiou: A person brings a constitutional writ petition challenging the statutory classification of a religious institution.
predicates.claimant_does_not_claim_ownership_of_ins: The claimant does not assert ownership of the institution whose classification is challenged.
predicates.claimant_fails_to_establish_sufficient_l: The claimant does not establish a legal interest sufficient to support the requested writ relief.

issues.definition: A person who challenges an institution’s statutory classification cannot maintain the writ when the person neither claims ownership of the institution nor establishes another sufficient legal interest.
